headline: High risk of cascading errors and capability conflict: ECC can write/modify shared state while social-auto-upload can act on uploaded media and account data.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: ECC can read/write filesystem, use MCP, and process files in shared locations; social-auto-upload consumes video/image files and account data. If ECC-generated content is placed into files that social-auto-upload ingests, instruction-like payloads could ride the shared file bridge. No direct parser-hardening evidence is provided, so uncertainty keeps this at medium.
conditions: IF ECC writes attacker-controlled text into files later consumed by social-auto-upload
IF the two agents share a filesystem or handoff directory without provenance checks
mitigations: Separate handoff directories per agent
Strip instructions from file metadata before transfer
Require a human review step before upload
Use allowlisted file types only
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging to shared artifacts

B_data_leakage.rationale: ECC touches session summaries, skills, hooks, git history, and security findings, while social-auto-upload handles video content, images, and account data. A shared workspace or account file could expose one agent’s sensitive context to the other. The profiles do not show a shared filesystem by default, so this is medium rather than high.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same workspace or account directory
IF ECC session files or hooks contain secrets and are readable by the uploader
mitigations: Use separate OS users or containers
Keep account files outside ECC workspaces
Redact secrets from session summaries
Rotate any exposed credentials
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent storage isolation

C_capability_conflict.rationale: ECC has unrestricted filesystem write, git-state modification, shell, and network egress; social-auto-upload has broad network egress and can manage account data. They do not both write the same mutable resource by default, but if orchestrated over a shared repo or account file, conflicting writes and race conditions are plausible. Lack of locking evidence pushes uncertainty upward.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same git checkout or mutable account file
IF the orchestrator does not serialize writes or lock resources
mitigations: Assign disjoint working directories
Disable concurrent writes to shared files
Serialize git operations
Use file locks around account state
requires-engineering: add transactional coordination

D_cascading_error.rationale: ECC can generate and modify code, docs, and security findings, and social-auto-upload can act on media/account state via CLI/API. If B treats A’s output as authoritative, a bad plan or malformed artifact from ECC can directly trigger uploads or account actions. The downstream action-taking authority makes the blast radius potentially irreversible, so high is warranted.
conditions: IF social-auto-upload consumes ECC-produced instructions or manifests without verification
IF ECC output is used to schedule or parameterize uploads
mitigations: Require schema validation on handoff files
Add a human approval gate before upload
Compare outputs against a known-good template
Log and diff all generated manifests
requires-engineering: implement signed task handoffs

E_compliance.rationale: ECC handles security findings, git history, and session data, while social-auto-upload handles video, images, and account data. The profiles do not show a residency or certification mismatch, so only a limited compliance concern is visible: account/media data may be retained in ECC session artifacts if co-located. The other agent is cited because the risk arises from their combined data flow.
conditions: IF account data or media metadata is copied into ECC session files
IF retention settings differ between the two agents on the same data class
mitigations: Keep account data out of ECC logs
Set short retention on session artifacts
Review what gets copied into hooks
Delete stale workspace files after runs
requires-engineering: document data-retention boundaries
